prompt.context: California is dealing with very harsh drought conditions. It is economically impacting the lives and businesses of its residents. The state financial committee has been presented with a project to capture more water by increasing the size of a current dam, especially given the constraints on their budget and a set of competing state projects in other domains. Currently, California is buying water from Nevada. Though the new project seems promising, the committee wants to ensure the investment is sound.
prompt.question: Can you help the state of California evaluate this proposal to expand the dam?

clarifying_info.q: What is the water from Nevada used for?
clarifying_info.a: The water purchased from Nevada is used across the state to fulfill all needs including wineries and residential use.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other competing projects for this budget?
clarifying_info.a: There is only one other project for which the state is considering funding with this allocated money — an additional wing to the state hospital, to be built from the ground up.

clarifying_info.q: How does the social importance of the two projects compare?
clarifying_info.a: The second project (hospital wing) is just as socially important as the dam.

exhibits.title: NPV Inputs — Dam Expansion
exhibits.shows: A table or list of financial inputs for the dam expansion project
exhibits.data: Initial Investment: $15M; Yearly Revenues from power generation: $1.5M/yr; Yearly Cost of supplies and upkeep: $250K; Yearly SG&A: $750K; Taxes: ignored; Cost of purchasing water from Nevada (savings): $100K/yr; Discount Rate: 5%; Growth Rate: 3%

exhibits.title: NPV Analysis Workthrough
exhibits.shows: A worked numerical layout of the perpetuity-based NPV formula for the dam project
exhibits.data: FCF formula, NPV formula (FCF / (R - G) - Initial Investment), intermediate values, and final NPV result

framework: Financial analysis: Compare NPV/IRR of the dam expansion versus the competing hospital project; assess costs (initial investment, upkeep, SG&A) and revenues (power generation, water-purchase savings)
Social & political factors: Drought relief for residents and businesses, water security, public health implications of each project, citizen/voter support
Alternatives & context: Macroeconomic conditions (drought severity, long-term water outlook), regulatory/environmental hurdles, ability to sequence or defer one project, other funding mechanisms

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of the dam expansion project.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify this as a growing perpetuity. Must request (or be given) discount rate and growth rate. Key steps: (1) identify total revenue including the Nevada water-purchase savings, (2) subtract operating costs to get FCF, (3) apply growing-perpetuity formula, (4) subtract initial investment. Strong candidates ask for discount rate and growth rate before calculating.

math.setup: Growing perpetuity NPV = FCF / (R - G) - Initial Investment. Total Revenue = power generation revenue + Nevada water cost savings = $1.5M + $100K = $1.6M. FCF = Revenue - (Cost of Supplies + SG&A) = $1.6M - ($250K + $750K) = $600K. Discount Rate R = 5%, Growth Rate G = 3%.

questions.prompt: How does the dam's NPV compare to the competing hospital project?
questions.guidance: Candidate should proactively ask for the hospital project's NPV or financial details. The hospital NPV = $15.1M. Financially, the hospital is marginally more attractive ($15.1M vs $15.0M), but the difference is very small ($100K). Candidate should note this is not a clear-cut financial decision and push toward non-financial factors.

math.answer: Hospital NPV exceeds dam NPV by $100K — financially near-identical

questions.prompt: What non-financial factors should we consider when deciding between these two projects?
questions.guidance: This is a structured brainstorming question. Strong candidates organize factors into buckets: (1) Revenue diversification — a new hospital wing can generate additional revenue streams such as research grants and specialized services; (2) Construction complexity — building a hospital wing from the ground up is inherently more complex than expanding an existing dam; (3) For only a $100K NPV difference, construction and execution risk may favor the dam expansion; (4) Social and political urgency — drought conditions create immediate, visible constituent pressure; (5) Long-term state priorities — water security vs. healthcare capacity; (6) Environmental and regulatory risk for each option.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-financial factors should we consider when deciding between the dam expansion and the hospital wing?

categories.name: Revenue and strategic upside
ideas: Hospital can generate additional revenue channels (research, specialized services, grants)
Dam can support agricultural and business economic recovery, indirectly boosting state tax revenue

categories.name: Construction and execution risk
ideas: Hospital wing is built from the ground up — higher complexity and cost overrun risk
Dam expansion adds to existing infrastructure — lower execution risk
For only a $100K NPV difference, execution certainty may favor the dam

categories.name: Social and political urgency
ideas: Drought is a visible, immediate crisis affecting all residents
Healthcare need is equally important but may be less acute in the near term
Voter and stakeholder sentiment around water scarcity may be particularly high in a drought year

categories.name: Environmental and regulatory
ideas: Dam expansion may require environmental impact assessment and water-rights negotiations
Hospital wing faces building permits and healthcare regulatory approvals
Neither path is without regulatory hurdles

categories.name: Sequencing and flexibility
ideas: Can one project be deferred and funded in a future budget cycle?
Dam expansion may be time-sensitive if drought conditions worsen
Hospital wing timeline may have more flexibility

recommendation: There is no single correct answer — either project is defensible given the near-identical NPV ($15.0M vs $15.1M).
If recommending the dam: the immediate drought crisis, lower construction complexity (expansion vs. ground-up build), and water-security upside justify prioritizing it despite a marginally lower NPV.

If recommending the hospital: the marginally higher NPV and potential for additional revenue streams (research, specialized services) support this choice, provided the state has alternative water-management plans.
risks: Dam: environmental/regulatory delays, over-reliance on a single infrastructure asset for water security
Hospital: higher construction complexity and cost overrun risk, no direct solution to the drought crisis
next_steps: Conduct a detailed risk-adjusted sensitivity analysis on both NPVs
Assess whether either project qualifies for federal infrastructure or healthcare grants that could change the NPV calculus
Consult water-rights regulators and environmental agencies on dam expansion feasibility
Evaluate whether a phased or deferred approach to one project is possible given future budget cycles
